title: Flame from flame
hookLine: is the one reborn the same person? like a flame lit from another flame, neither the same nor different (Milinda, Book 2)
carry: owing its light to the one before

cards: If a name is only a name for parts, the king has a sharper question waiting. Buddhists speak of rebirth. When a life ends and another begins, he asks, is the one born the same as the one who died, or someone else?
It's a trap with two doors. Say the same, and there's a fixed self after all, carried from body to body. Say someone else, and why should anyone care what happens to that stranger?
Nagasena takes neither door. Neither the same, he says, nor another. And then, as always, he reaches for something you could hold in your hand.

teach.b: First, a lamp through the night.

teach.h: A FLAME LIT, AND NOTHING PASSES OVER.
teach.b: If a man lights a lamp and it burns all night, Nagasena asks, is the flame in the first watch the same as the flame in the middle watch? No, says the king. And the last watch?
Not the same either. Then were there several lamps? No, the light burned all night from the same lamp.
Just so, says Nagasena: one moment arises as another passes, and the line runs on, neither the same nor another. Second, a lamp lit from a lamp.
Elsewhere in the book the king asks whether rebirth happens without anything passing over. Yes, Nagasena says. When one lamp is lit from another, no little piece of the first flame travels across.
Yet the second burns, and it wouldn't without the first.

teach.h: A VERSE LEARNED FROM A TEACHER.
teach.b: Third, a verse from a teacher. The king learned verses from his teacher as a boy. Did the verse transmigrate into him?
No. Yet he has it, because of the teacher. Fourth, why the image matters.
A flame lit from a flame is not a soul moving house, and not a stranger either. It's a cause and what it causes, close enough to be responsible for, open enough to change.
And the night-long lamp shows it within one life too: on that picture, the person who started this lesson is already a later flame of the same lamp.
In the Theravada telling, what carries on is not a thing but a continuing, each flame owing its light to the one before.

how: Theravada teachers often explain rebirth with Nagasena's lamp images from the Questions of King Milinda: a continuing of causes, neither the same person nor a different one, with no soul passing across.

o: a light that must never be allowed to go out
a soul carried whole from one body to the next
a flame lit from a flame, with nothing passing over

games.q: flame from flame: tap the pairs.
p: not the same flame, yet one lamp
a lamp lit from a lamp
a verse learned from a teacher

s: Nagasena says the one reborn is exactly the same person
he says neither the same nor another.
when one lamp lights another, a piece of the first flame travels over
Nagasena's point is that nothing passes across, yet the second is lit because of the first.
the king learned verses from his teacher without the verses transmigrating
Nagasena uses that as a picture of rebirth with nothing passing over.

games.q: you're Nagasena. the king asks: is the one who is reborn the same person as the one who died, or someone else?
games.why: he refuses both doors and reaches for a lamp: the flame at dusk and the flame at dawn are not the same, yet it is one lamp burning all night.

practice: If you can do it safely, light one candle from another and watch the new flame catch; if not, bring the picture to mind. Then sit with the breath: each one arises from the one before, and none of them is the same breath.

wordCard.voice: Lamp. Nagasena's image for rebirth: nothing passes from one flame to the next, yet the light burns on.

orig.note: Pali and Sanskrit: lamp. the image Nagasena keeps returning to for rebirth.

carryVoice: Your line: owing its light to the one before. Neither the same, nor another. Day eight hundred sixty-nine.
